title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: At Bald Hills, the estate of Prince Nikolai Andreevich Bolkonsky, the arrival of young Prince Andrei and his wife was expected any day, but this didn't disrupt the old prince's rigid household routine. General-in-Chief Prince Nikolai Andreevich—nicknamed "the King of Prussia" in society—had been living at his country estate continuously since Emperor Paul had exiled him there, together with his daughter, Princess Mary, and her companion, Mademoiselle Bourienne. Though the new reign had made him free to return to the capitals, he continued to live in the country, remarking that anyone who wanted to see him could make the hundred-mile trip from Moscow to Bald Hills, while he himself needed nobody and nothing. He liked to say there are only two sources of human vice—idleness and superstition—and only two virtues—activity and intelligence. He personally oversaw his daughter's education, and to develop these two virtues in her, gave her lessons in algebra and geometry until she was twenty and organized her life so that every hour was accounted for. He himself was perpetually busy: writing his memoirs, solving problems in higher mathematics, turning snuffboxes on a lathe, working in the garden, or supervising the construction that was always underway on his estate. Since regularity is the first condition of productivity, regularity in his household was maintained to the highest degree of precision. He always came to meals not just at the same hour but at the same minute. With everyone around him, from his daughter down to the servants, the prince was sharp and unfailingly demanding—not out of cruelty, but with a severity that inspired the kind of fear and respect that few genuinely cruel men could have commanded. Although he was retired and no longer wielded political influence, every senior official appointed to the province felt duty-bound to pay him a visit, and they waited in his lofty antechamber—alongside the architect, the gardener, and Princess Mary—until the prince appeared at precisely the appointed time. Everyone in that waiting room experienced the same mix of respect and dread when the enormously tall study door swung open to reveal the small figure of the old man: powdered wig, small withered hands, and bushy gray eyebrows that, when he frowned, could hide the sharp gleam of his youthful, piercing eyes.

On the morning of the day the young couple was expected, Princess Mary entered the antechamber at the usual time for the morning greeting, crossing herself nervously and repeating a silent prayer. She came in like this every morning, and every morning she prayed the encounter would go smoothly.
An old powdered manservant sitting in the antechamber stood quietly and said in a whisper: "Please go in."

Through the door came the steady hum of a lathe. The princess timidly pushed open the door, which moved silently on its hinges. She paused at the threshold. The prince was working at the lathe and, after a quick glance, went on with what he was doing.

The enormous study was full of objects clearly in constant use. A large table strewn with books and plans, tall glass-fronted bookcases with keys in their locks, a high standing desk with an open exercise book on it, the lathe with tools at the ready and shavings scattered around—everything spoke of continuous, varied, disciplined activity. The rhythmic motion of his small foot in a silver-embroidered Tartar boot, and the firm pressure of his lean, sinewy hand, showed that the prince still possessed all the endurance and energy of a hardy old age. After a few more turns of the lathe, he removed his foot from the pedal, wiped his chisel, dropped it into a leather pouch attached to the lathe, and walked to the table to greet his daughter. He never gave his children a blessing, so he simply offered his bristly, unshaven cheek and, looking at her with tender attention, said sternly:
"Feeling well? Good. Sit down." He took the exercise book of geometry lessons he had written himself and pulled up a chair with his foot.
"For tomorrow!" he said, quickly finding the right page and marking a section with a hard fingernail, scratching from one paragraph to the next.
The princess bent over the exercise book on the table.
"Wait—here's a letter for you," the old man said suddenly, pulling a letter in a woman's handwriting from a bag hanging above the table and tossing it to her.
Red blotches appeared on the princess's face at the sight of the letter. She snatched it up quickly and bent her head over it.
"From Heloise?" the prince asked with a cold smile that revealed his still-sound, yellowish teeth.
"Yes, it's from Julie," the princess replied with a timid glance and a shy smile.
"I'll let two more letters pass, but the third one I'm reading," the prince said sternly. "I'm afraid you write a lot of nonsense. I'll read the third!"
"Read this one if you like, Father," said the princess, blushing even more and holding out the letter.
"The third, I said the third!" the prince snapped, pushing the letter away. He leaned his elbows on the table and drew the geometry exercise book toward him.

"Now then, young lady," he began, bending over the book close to his daughter and resting his arm on the back of her chair, so that she found herself enveloped on all sides by the sharp scent of old age and tobacco that she had known all her life. "Now then—these triangles are equal. Please observe that the angle ABC..."

The princess stared with frightened eyes at her father's face, which glittered with intensity right next to hers. The red patches came and went on her cheeks, and it was obvious she understood nothing and was so terrified that her fear would block any comprehension of his explanations, no matter how clear. Whether the fault lay with the teacher or the student, the same thing happened every day: the princess's eyes glazed over, she could neither see nor hear, conscious only of her stern father's withered face close to hers, his breath and his smell, able to think of nothing but escaping to her own room to work out the problem in peace. The old man would lose his composure, noisily shoving his chair back and forth, struggling to hold his temper—and nearly always failing. He would scold her, and sometimes hurl the exercise book across the room.
The princess gave a wrong answer.
"Now, isn't she a fool!" the prince shouted, shoving the book aside and turning sharply away. But he immediately stood up, paced the room, gently touched his daughter's hair, and sat down again.
He pulled his chair closer and resumed his explanation.

"This won't do, Princess, it won't do," he said as Princess Mary closed the exercise book with tomorrow's lesson and prepared to leave. "Mathematics is essential, young lady! I don't want you turning out like those silly society women. Stick with it and you'll come to enjoy it." He patted her cheek. "It'll drive all the foolishness out of your head."
She turned to go, but he stopped her with a gesture and took an uncut book from the high desk.
"Here's some sort of Key to the Mysteries that your Heloise sent you. Religion! I don't interfere with anyone's beliefs... I've had a look at it. Take it. Well—go on, go."
He patted her on the shoulder and personally closed the door behind her.

Princess Mary returned to her room wearing the sad, anxious expression that rarely left her face and that made her plain, sickly features seem even plainer. She sat down at her writing desk, which was surrounded by miniature portraits and cluttered with books and papers. The princess was as messy as her father was orderly. She set down the geometry book and eagerly broke the seal on her letter. It was from her closest childhood friend—the very same Julie Karagina who had been at the Rostovs' name-day party.
Julie wrote in French:

Dear and precious Friend, How terrible and frightening it is to be separated! Though I tell myself that half my life and half my happiness are wrapped up in you, and that despite the distance between us our hearts are joined by unbreakable bonds, my heart rebels against fate, and despite all the pleasures and distractions around me, I cannot shake a certain secret sorrow that has lived in my heart ever since we parted. Why can't we be together as we were last summer, in your big study, on the blue sofa—the sofa where we shared our secrets? Why can't I draw fresh moral strength from your gaze, as I did three months ago—that gaze so gentle, calm, and searching, which I loved so much and seem to see before me now as I write?

Having read this far, Princess Mary sighed and glanced at the mirror on her right. It reflected a thin, graceless figure and a gaunt face. Her eyes, always sad, now looked with particular hopelessness at her own reflection. "She flatters me," the princess thought, looking away and continuing to read. But Julie was not flattering her friend. The princess's eyes—large, deep, and luminous, as though warm shafts of light sometimes radiated from them—were so beautiful that despite the plainness of her face, they often lent her a magnetism more powerful than conventional beauty. But the princess never saw the beautiful expression of her own eyes—the look they had when she wasn't thinking about herself. Like everyone, her face took on a forced, unnatural expression as soon as she looked in a mirror. She continued reading:

All Moscow talks of nothing but war. One of my two brothers is already abroad; the other is with the Guards, who are about to march for the frontier. Our dear Emperor has left Petersburg, and it's believed he intends to expose his precious person to the dangers of war. God grant that the Corsican monster who is destroying the peace of Europe may be overthrown by the angel whom the Almighty, in His goodness, has given us as our sovereign! To say nothing of my brothers, this war has robbed me of one of the bonds dearest to my heart. I mean young Nikolai Rostov, who was so passionately enthusiastic that he couldn't bear to remain idle and has left the university to join the army. I will confess to you, dear Mary, that despite his extreme youth, his departure for the army was a great sorrow for me. This young man, of whom I told you last summer, is so noble-spirited and full of that genuine youthfulness one so rarely finds anymore among our old men of twenty—and above all, he is so honest and has so much heart. He is so pure and poetic that my relationship with him, brief as it was, has been one of the sweetest comforts to my poor heart, which has already suffered so much. Someday I'll tell you about our parting and everything that was said. It's all still too fresh. Ah, dear friend, you're lucky not to know these sharp joys and sorrows. You are fortunate, because the sorrows are usually stronger! I know perfectly well that Count Nikolai is too young ever to be more than a friend to me, but this sweet friendship, this poetic, pure bond, was exactly what my heart needed. But enough of this! The main news, the talk of all Moscow, is the death of old Count Bezukhov and his inheritance. Can you imagine! The three princesses received almost nothing, Prince Vasili got nothing at all, and it's Monsieur Pierre who has inherited everything and has been officially recognized as legitimate—so he is now Count Bezukhov and the owner of the greatest fortune in Russia. People say Prince Vasili played a thoroughly contemptible role in the whole affair and went back to Petersburg completely humiliated.

I'll admit I don't understand much about wills and inheritance, but I do know that ever since this young man—whom we all used to know as plain Monsieur Pierre—became Count Bezukhov and owner of one of the largest fortunes in Russia, I've been greatly entertained watching how the tone and manners of mothers with marriageable daughters, and of the young ladies themselves, have changed toward him. Though, between you and me, he always struck me as a rather unremarkable fellow. Since for the past two years people have amused themselves finding husbands for me—most of whom I don't even know—the Moscow matchmaking rumor mill now speaks of me as the future Countess Bezukhova. But you'll understand I have no interest in that title. Speaking of marriages: did you know that a while ago that universal busybody Anna Mikhaylovna told me, in the strictest confidence, about a marriage plan for you? It involves none other than Prince Vasili's son Anatole, whom they hope to reform through marriage to someone wealthy and distinguished—and you are the one his family has chosen. I don't know how you'll feel about it, but I thought it my duty to tell you. He's said to be very handsome and an absolute rogue. That's all I've been able to find out about him.

But enough gossip. I'm at the bottom of my second sheet of paper, and Mama has sent for me to go dine at the Apraksins'. Read the mystical book I'm sending you—it's an enormous success here. Though there are things in it that are hard for our feeble human minds to grasp, it is a wonderful book that calms and elevates the soul. Farewell! Give my respects to your father and my regards to Mademoiselle Bourienne. I embrace you as I love you.
JULIE
P.S. Send me news of your brother and his charming little wife.

The princess sat thinking for a while, a thoughtful smile on her face, her luminous eyes lighting up until her expression was completely transformed. Then she rose abruptly and, with her heavy step, went to the writing table. She took out a sheet of paper and her hand flew rapidly across it. This was her reply, also in French:

Dear and precious Friend, Your letter of the 13th brought me great joy. So you still love me, my romantic Julie? The separation you complain about so bitterly seems not to have had its usual effect on you. You speak of your loneliness—but what should I say, I who am cut off from everyone dear to me? Ah, if we didn't have religion to comfort us, life would be so bleak. Why do you think I would judge your feelings for that young man harshly? In such matters I am strict only with myself. I understand such feelings in others, and though I've never experienced them, I can neither approve nor condemn them. It only seems to me that Christian love—love of neighbor, love of one's enemy—is worthier, sweeter, and more beautiful than the feelings that a handsome young man's eyes can awaken in a romantic and loving young girl like you.

The news of Count Bezukhov's death reached us before your letter, and my father was deeply affected. He says the count was the last representative but one of the great century, and that his own turn is next—though he'll do everything he can to postpone it as long as possible. God spare us from that terrible misfortune!

I can't agree with you about Pierre, whom I've known since he was a child. He always seemed to me to have an excellent heart, and that is the quality I value most in people. As for his inheritance and Prince Vasili's role in it—how sad for both of them. Ah, my dear friend, how terribly true are our divine Savior's words: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of God. I pity Prince Vasili, but I feel even sorrier for Pierre. So young, and weighed down with such wealth—what temptations lie ahead of him! If anyone asked me what I desire most on earth, it would be to be poorer than the poorest beggar. A thousand thanks, dear friend, for the book you've sent, which is enjoying such success in Moscow. But since you tell me it contains things our weak minds cannot understand alongside its good things, it seems rather pointless to spend time on what is incomprehensible and therefore fruitless. I have never understood why some people enjoy confusing their minds with mystical books that only awaken doubt and inflame the imagination, giving them a tendency toward exaggeration entirely contrary to Christian simplicity. Let us read the Epistles and the Gospels instead. Let us not try to penetrate their mysteries, for how can we—wretched sinners that we are—presume to understand the terrible, holy secrets of Providence while we remain in this flesh, which is an impenetrable veil between us and the Eternal? Let us confine ourselves to the sublime rules our divine Savior left for our guidance here on earth. Let us try to follow them, and let us trust that the less we allow our feeble human minds to wander, the more we shall please God, who rejects all knowledge not from Him; and the less we try to fathom what He has chosen to conceal from us, the sooner He will reveal it through His divine Spirit.

My father has not spoken to me of a suitor, but has only mentioned that he received a letter and is expecting a visit from Prince Vasili. Regarding this marriage proposal, I will tell you, dear sweet friend, that I consider marriage a divine institution to which we must submit. However painful it may be, should the Almighty place upon me the duties of wife and mother, I will try to fulfill them as faithfully as I can, without troubling myself to examine my feelings toward whomever He may give me as a husband.

I've had a letter from my brother announcing his imminent arrival at Bald Hills with his wife. This pleasure will be short-lived, however, as he will be leaving again to take part in this terrible war into which we have been drawn—God knows how or why. Not only where you are, at the heart of affairs and society, but even here, amid farmwork and the tranquility of nature that city people think defines the countryside—here too the rumors of war are heard and felt painfully. My father talks of nothing but marches and countermarches, things I understand nothing about. And the day before yesterday, during my daily walk through the village, I witnessed a heartbreaking scene.... It was a column of conscripts drafted from our people, setting off to join the army. You should have seen the state of the mothers, wives, and children of the men who were leaving. You should have heard the weeping. It seems as if humanity has forgotten the laws of our divine Savior, who preached love and the forgiveness of wrongs—and that people now believe the highest merit lies in the skill of killing one another.
Farewell, dear and kind friend. May our divine Savior and His most Holy Mother keep you in Their holy and all-powerful care!
MARY

"Ah, so you're sending a letter, Princess? I've already sent mine. I wrote to my poor mother," said Mademoiselle Bourienne with a smile, speaking quickly in her pleasant, melodious voice with its rolling r's. She brought into Princess Mary's earnest, sorrowful world a completely different atmosphere—carefree, lighthearted, and self-satisfied.

"Princess, I should warn you," she added, lowering her voice and clearly enjoying the sound of it, speaking with exaggerated affectation, "the prince has been scolding Mikhail Ivanovich. He's in a terrible mood—very grim. Be prepared."
"Ah, dear friend," Princess Mary replied, "I've asked you never to tell me what mood my father is in. I don't allow myself to judge him, and I wouldn't want others to either."

The princess glanced at her watch and, seeing that she was five minutes late starting her practice on the clavichord, hurried into the sitting room with an anxious expression. Between twelve and two o'clock, according to the day's fixed schedule, the prince rested and the princess played the clavichord.
